Jaina Rāmāyaṇas
------------------------------------------
The two great epics—the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata—have made such a deep impression on the Indian मिन्द् that the core part of the stories in them have percolated into the literature of other religions of Indian origin like जैनिस्म् and बुद्धिस्म्.
In the Jaina tradition, there is no single रामायण as such. Eleven well-known Jaina works, of fairly early period, deal with the story of राम. Out of these, the Paumacariyam of Vimala Sūri (circa A.

-500) in प्राकृत् is the most famous.
Evolution of राम story and allied literature continued for several centuries (7th to the 14th). Some of the works were in Sanskrit and some in प्राकृत् and Apabhraṁśa (crude forms of Sanskrit and local variations) languages.
Vimala Sūri declares that the Rāmā-yaṇa stories (of the Hindus) are full of lies, absurdities and contradictions. To remove these, he undertook the composition of Paumacariyam! (Pauma = पद्म = राम.)
Though he follows the main outline of वाल्मीकि’s story he has made several changes, giving the whole work a Jaina colour. For instance: राम never killed the golden deer or वालि. He never ate meat. The vānaras were actually विद्याधरस् (a race of supernatural beings possessing extraordinary powers) and not monkeys. The राक्षसस् were highly cultured persons. वालि handed over his kingdom to his younger brother सुग्रीव and became a Jain monk. It is लक्ष्मण who killed रावण. लक्ष्मण ultimately went to हेल्ल् since he refused to become a Jaina monk whereas कैकेयी, सीता and other ladies became Jaina nuns.
Many other changes also have been introduced into the body of the story, like सीता being the daughter of रावण and मण्डोदरी, लक्ष्मण killing the śūdra ascetic Śambūka by mistake and so on.
It is obvious that these Rāmāyaṇas or राम-stories were used more to propagate जैनिस्म् than to narrate the story itself.

Jainism
------------------------------------------
One of the religions of the world—great in principles though the number of adherents is small—is जैनिस्म्. It is sometimes considered as a ‘rebel child’ of Hinduism—if the word हिन्दुइस्म् is taken in a geographical sense—or as an independent religion, though allied with it closely.
The Jains claim great antiquity to their religion, the earliest Tīrthaṅkara—propagator of spiritual wisdom—being the sage Ṛṣabhadeva mentioned as an ancient sage even in the Viṣṇupurāṇa. Recorded history, however, recognises only two: पार्श्वनाथ (8th century B. C.) and महावीर (599-527 B. C.).
Mahāvīra (also known as Vardha-māna) left behind him a well-organised religious Order of Jaina मोन्क्स्.
Due to the missionary activities of the Jaina teachers, the religion attracted kings and nobles as well as the common people and spread to many parts of India. The Mauryan emperor Candragupta is said to have become a convert to जैनिस्म् and settled in Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa (of Karnataka) during his last days.
Jainism has a philosophy and a way of life which is in consonance with that philosophy. It recognises two fundamental principles—the jīvatattva (living beings) and the ajīvatattva (non-living objects). These two principles come into contact with one another and forge certain energies that bring forth birth, various experiences of life and death.
This process can be stopped and the energies already forged can be destroyed by a course of discipline leading to salvation.
The prescribed ethical code is fivefold: अहिṁसा (non-violence), सत्य (truth), अस्तेय (non-stealing), ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy) and अपरिग्रह (non-acceptance of gifts).
Since certain relaxations are allowed to householders in the observance of these vows out of necessity, they become ‘aṇuvrata’ (‘the small vow’). But for मोन्क्स् their observance is absolute. They therefore become ‘mahāvratas’ (‘great vows’) in their case.
The अनेकान्तवाद or syādvāda is an important aspect of Jaina philosophy.
See ANEKĀNTAVĀDA.
